HEADLINE: Allan gets $90b gig in Andrews cabinet
TEXT:
Jacinta Allan has emerged as the big winner in re-elected Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews' cabinet reshuffle, taking on a super ministry embracing the Labor government's huge transport project pipeline, roads and public transport.

Ms Allan leads an "all-female transport team" with Jaala Pulford becoming the minister for roads, as well as fishing and boating, and new cabinet member Melissa Horne taking Ms Allen's old job as minister for transport, ports and freight.

Ms Allan's primary responsibility will be the Andrews' government's $90 billion transport pipeline, including level crossing removals, the North East Link, West Gate Tunnel, Metro Tunnel and the as-yet-uncommitted Suburban Rail Loop.

As well as a big focus on building infrastructure, the new cabinet focuses on social policy, crime and family violence. Mr Andrews rated family violence as Victoria's "biggest law and order challenge" after winning re-election in a landslide over the Liberal-National coalition led by Matthew Guy, who stood down on Wednesday.

On Thursday Liberal leadership aspirant John Pesutto slipped 156 votes behind his Labor opponent John Ormond Kennedy in a knife-edge count. Shadow Treasurer Michael O'Brien has also declared his hand, while shadow energy minister David Southwick and member for Gembrook Brad Battin are also possible contenders.

Tim Pallas continues as Treasurer, adding responsibility for economic development and industrial relations, assisted by Robin Scott. Deputy Premier James Merlino continues as education minister, with 1300 schools upgrades, 100 new schools and the rollout of a program providing pre-school for all three-year olds on his to-do list. Lily d'Ambrosio continues as Energy Minister, with the task of rolling out solar panels on 700,000 houses.

Marlene Kairouz becomes Minister for Suburban Development - "to ensure our growing outer suburbs get the services they need" - and retains responsibility for gaming and consumer affairs.

Although the Coalition's law and order campaign failed to shift votes its way, the Andrews government has recognised the potency of crime - especially youth crime - as an issue by making improving community safety and crime prevention a priority for the new Department of Justice and Community Safety.

Jill Hennessy switches from health to become Attorney-General, responsible for implementing "Australia's toughest bail laws" and ensuring "we have the statute book we need to help keep Victorians safe". She will also be minister for workplace safety. Lisa Neville continues as police minister with additional responsibility for emergency services, overseeing the recruitment and training of 3135 new police. She continues as the Minister for Water. Ben Carroll becomes Minister for Crime Prevention and Victim Support, Corrections and Youth Justice.

New cabinet member Gabrielle Williams is the Minister for the Prevention of Family Violence. "We will continue our record investment to combat family violence and keep women and children safe," Mr Andrews said.

Ms Williams will also be the Minister for Women and, as the youngest member of cabinet, the Minister for Youth. Luke Donnellan moves from roads to child protection, disability and ageing.

Jenny Mikakos becomes Minister for Health, with large hospital building and free dental health programs to roll out. Martin Foley continues as Minister for Mental Health, responsible for Australia's first royal commission into mental health - a major cause of crime.

Richard Wynne remains Planning Minister, with housing and multicultural affairs added to his workload. Former attorney-general Martin Pakula becomes Minister for Jobs, Innovation and Trade, as well as Sport and Major Events, and remains Minister for Racing. Gayle Tierney will be Minister for Training, Skills and Higher Education, responsible for the roll out of free TAFE.

The government has recognised the potency of crime as an issue.

HEADLINE: APRA's Byres needed more mongrel on CBA
TEXT:
APRA chairman Wayne Byres said he and his senior management should have shown more "mongrel" and backed the "gut feel" of his staff, who identified suspected breaches by Commonwealth Bank in the lead up to the AUSTRAC money laundering debacle.

Mr Byres, appearing at the Hayne inquiry yesterday, also revealed APRA will release early next year a new model for executive remuneration and rewrite its prudential standards.

HEADLINE: AFR Magazine Macquarie exit: Last day for Nicholas Moore
TEXT:
Ask Nicholas Moore what he will do next after his last day today at Macquarie Group and he describes something that sounds uncannily like a miniature version of Macquarie.

"One of the many great things about Macquarie, obviously, is the people and the new ideas and the new businesses that we develop and work with clients who are developing over the years," he says.

"I'd like to continue to be exposed to new ideas and people in particular, who have got passions and have got things they want to fulfil, and help them, to the extent that I can."

Of course, whatever he does it will have to be on top of his existing commitments including the chairman of the Sydney Opera House Trust and Screen Australia, a director of the Centre for Independent Studies and chairman of the University of NSW Business School Advisory Council.

Moore's idea of a one-man investment house sounds similar to the path followed by his predecessor Allan Moss, who became an active investor in technology start-ups, offshore private companies and industrial property after handing over to Moore in mid-2008.

When the handover from Moss to Moore was announced in February 2008 Macquarie shares were trading at about $60 each. The global financial crisis meant it took until May 2014 for Macquarie to regain the $60 a share mark.

Moore's performance through the GFC defined his 10½ years as chief executive of Macquarie. He led the evolution of the group's business model from a reliance on volatile markets-facing businesses such as investment banking to a more stable earnings machine with several annuities-style businesses.

He leaves the building on Friday with an impressive financial track record against his name. The total shareholder return since his first day as CEO is 300 per cent. Annuity-style business now dominates the profit and international income is 67 per cent of the total.

Under Moore's leadership, Macquarie made several counter-cyclical acquisitions including Constellation Energy, Delaware Investments, AIG planes, Cargill's North American power and gas business and the Green Investment Bank, now called Green Investment Group. Macquarie is now the third largest energy trader in the United States.

Moore has immense confidence in his successor, Shemara Wikramanayake, who has worked at Macquarie since 1987. For the past decade Wikramanayake has been running the funds business which now has $550 billion in funds under management.

Moore says working alongside her made him very comfortable with her "intelligence, work ethic, analytical ability and judgment".

"I am very pleased in terms of the recognition that Shemara has [in financial markets] in terms of her capability, her competence, her knowledge of the business and her ability," he says.

Wikramanayake says Moore will be remembered for distilling the Macquarie culture into three words - opportunity, accountability and integrity.

"I think he's also taught me about constantly evolving and challenging what we do," she says. "I don't think any individual has made an impact on the organisation the way Nicholas has, moving us into new frontiers. He's never stopped going forward."

During his tenure as CEO Moore earned the respect of his peers and of the political class. Both the Treasurer Josh Frydenberg and shadow treasurer Chris Bowen were full of praise for Moore during interviews with The Australian Financial Review in the lead-up to his departure as CEO.

Other former politicians to give bouquets were former Coalition government treasurers Peter Costello and Joe Hockey and former Labor premier and foreign minister Bob Carr.

Bowen says Moore has been a valuable sounding board over the years. "He would always have the national interests in mind, he would not just talk his own book," Bowen says.

Shayne Elliott, chief executive of ANZ Banking Group, says Moore was one of the first people to reach out to him when he was appointed CEO of ANZ. "We had a cup of tea [green] and he generously shared his thoughts, experiences and learnings from being CEO," he says. "I found it to be one of the engaging and inspiring talks I had at the time."

Westpac chief executive Brian Hartzer says Moore "blends a level of market experience, broad perspective and high intellect with humility and curiosity that makes him a great risk manager".

Chris Knoblanche, who sits on the board of the Opera House Trust with Moore and is a former head of investment banking at Citi, says meetings with Moore, when they did business together, were always professional but he knew it was all about the business flows between the two banks.

"You were not going to amble in for a cup of tea and talk about the weather," he says. "We were there to talk business and he wanted to make sure the business was two ways. It was a case of what business are you giving us and what can we do for you."

Moore plans to spend more time with his family and will continue to pursue his two favourite sports - jogging and swimming. Look out for him in the Macquarie-sponsored Big Swim in January, which involves swimming 2.8 kilometres from Palm Beach to Whale Beach in Sydney.

Read Nicholas Moore's last interview as Macquarie Bank's CEO in full in The Australian Financial Review Magazine inside today's Financial Review paper and at afr.com

HEADLINE: PM urges China, US to end brutal trade war
TEXT:
Phillip Coorey | Buenos Aires | Scott Morrison has implored China and the US to use this weekend's G20 leaders' summit to end their trade war, saying the dispute is now posing a real threat to the global economy. The Prime Minister left behind his own troubled government and flew to the Argentine capital for the summit seen as the most critical G20 since the global financial crisis a decade ago.

HEADLINE: Labor heat over Adani green light
TEXT:
State and federal Labor leaders have refused to back Adani's $2 billion Queensland Carmichael mine after the Indian company said it would fund the project itself, with construction planned to begin before Christmas.

The decision to give the financial green light for the mine, which has been the lightning rod for anti-coal environmentalists for the past decade, together with climate change and energy policy are expected to dominate next year's federal election.

Labor leader Bill Shorten is under pressure to scrap approvals for the Adani project if Labor wins the next poll, due in mid-May.

Mr Shorten, who is wedged between anti-coal forces in his party and the need to win seats in Queensland at the election, dodged comments on the Adani plan yesterday, leaving opposition resources spokesman Jason Clare to point out that the Indian company had a history of not delivering on its promises.

The issue of Adani and climate change is expected to be front and centre of Labor's national c

onference next month, with Mr Shorten pushing a resurrected National Energy Guarantee as a solution to a decade of uncertainty over energy policy.

Queensland Premier Annastacia Palaszczuk, who used to be an enthusiastic supporter of the Carmichael mine but backflipped on approving a federal loan for the project during last year's state election campaign, did not endorse the Adani project go-ahead yesterday, only noting that "no taxpayer money would go towards this project".

Environmental activists have vowed to fight against the mine for the life of the project.

After eight years of bitterly fought court challenges from environmental activists and delayed approvals, Adani Mining chief executive Lucas Dow on Thursday said the company had finally reached financial close on the project, which could start exporting coal by the end of 2020.

The decision could prove a catalyst for opening up the frontier Galilee Basin, with other big coal mines expected to follow including GVK/Hancock Coal's two mines and MacMines' recently approved $6.7 billion China Stone project. It will also be welcomed by pro-coal activists in the Morrison government, including federal Resources Minister Matt Canavan.

Senator Canavan hit out at environmental activists who yesterday linked the Adani project with wildfires which are burning across Queensland.

"The activists and the Greens just do more damage with stuff like this because people get the heebie geebies with this," Senator Canavan said.

Senator Canavan said the thermal coal from Adani's mine - which will be used to power the company's power stations in India - was part of the solution to global warming, helping cut air pollution and lowering carbon emissions.

"This is not a debate about climate change. It's a debate about how we get carbon emissions down and cleaner fossil fuels is the way to do this and Adani is part of it," he said.

India, one of the fastest-growing economies in the world, has also become an important trading partner in recent years. Australian Conservation Foundation chief executive Kelly O'Shannesey said the "Stop Adani Movement" would fight the proposed Carmichael mine every step of the way.

"There is too much at stake. Millions of Australians have shown up and spoken out against this climate wrecking mine. They will keep on until we stop Adani," she said.

Ms Palaszczuk suggested Adani may struggle to get access to Aurizon's existing coal network to export coal through the Abbot Point coal terminal near Bowen in North Queensland.

"This appears to be a very different proposal to previous announcements that have been made in relation to this project," she said in a statement.

"In addition to the change in scope, this announcement involves a rail corridor that will require, among other things, agreements with existing users and the operators."

Mr Clare was sceptical about Adani's move.

"They have made plenty of announcements before. Labor's position has been clear. There shouldn't be a dollar of taxpayer money spent propping up the project," a spokesperson for Mr Clare said.

"We said the project as first proposed wouldn't stack up, and it didn't. We said it wouldn't create jobs that were promised to Queenslanders, and it won't."

Last month, Adani announced it would scale back the size and scope of the Carmichael mine - trimming it back from the 60 million tonne $16.5 billion mega-mine, to a more manageable 10 to 15 million tonnes a year, with the potential to be scaled up to 27 million tonnes a year.

Adani, which has already spent $3.3 billion in Australia, said the capital cost of the scaled-back project would come in at around $2 billion. They had been talking to international banks to finance the project, but Mr Dow said this was no longer needed.

He said the "sharpening" of the mine plan had kept operating costs to a minimum and the construction and the operation of the thermal coal mine will now begin.

"We've pulled the trigger and we've got finance and we're ready to go," Mr Dow said in an interview with The Australian Financial Review.

"It has been a long time coming and we're obviously very excited about announcing this so we can get on and this and deliver the jobs for the people who have stood alongside us all this time. I'm desperate to have these jobs come into the northern part of Queensland."

Mr Dow said the project, which now only needs final management plans signed off by state and federal governments, would be funded by parent company Adani Group's finances rather than externally by a bank.

"It's akin to Rio Tinto or BHP funding the project. It's come from group Treasury. They have got it secured," he said.

When asked whether Adani Group had to borrow money from international banks to help fund projects including the Carmichael mine, Mr Dow said he "didn't want to speculate".

"That's a matter for group treasury. The important part for us is Carmichael mine and railway is fully funded and we're in a position to be able to get on with it. We're very much masters of our own destiny."

Mr Dow, a former BHP executive, said any future scaling up of the mine and rail to 27 million tonnes would be funded by profits from the mine's initial production. Mr Dow said the announcement should remove any doubt about the Carmichael project stacking up, saying it remains within the first quartile of the global cost curve.

Adani said the Carmichael project will deliver more than 1500 direct jobs on the mine and rail projects during the initial ramp-up and construction phase and will support thousands more indirect jobs.

This is a long way from the 10,000 jobs that had been touted for the project in recent incarnations.

HEADLINE: Amazon cuts Woolies, Coles lunch
TEXT:
Amazon has launched an assault on Australia's $100 billion food and grocery market, prompting complaints from Woolworths that multinational suppliers are favouring the e-commerce giant with cheaper prices on brands such as Colgate, Huggies, Omo and Finish.

After stepping up pressure on Woolworths and Coles by adding food and beverages to its non-food pantry range last month, Amazon Australia is now undercutting the dominant supermarket chains by as much as 50 per cent on household staples and quickly capturing a foothold in the market.

Woolworths sources said Amazon.com.au was selling food and groceries at lower prices than Australia's largest supermarket chain on a number of products and in some cases at prices below Woolworths' purchase price.

"The question is are they selling below cost, which would be inappropriate. Do they have global [pricing] deals or are Australian suppliers giving them better deals than the major supermarket chains - it's not clear," a Woolworths source told The Australian Financial Review.

Woolworths, which accounts for about 38 per cent of the food and grocery market, plans to seek a "please explain" from suppliers early in the new year.

Suppliers found to be giving Amazon better terms risk having their brands removed from shelves and replaced with rival brands and private label brands if sales of their products underperform in Woolworths stores.

Under the Food and Grocery Code of Conduct retailers can no longer arbitrarily delist products from shelves. However, if sales fail to meet targets retailers can remove products from shelves for genuine commercial reasons or as part of a range review after giving suppliers written notice of the purpose of the review and the criteria governing their decisions.

The risk for suppliers is that if they are delisted or scaled back by Woolworths and Coles, which together account for 69 per cent of the market, they become more reliant on Amazon. Amazon has less than 1 per cent of the online food and grocery market, which grew 39.7 per cent over the last 12 months, according to Nielsen.

At Woolworths' annual meeting in 2017 chairman Gordon Cairns warned food and grocery suppliers could "cut their own throats" by selling on Amazon and losing control over prices and losing business with the major chains.

"I'm not telling them what they should do, but before they step into the breach they should perhaps consider the long-term ramifications," said Mr Cairns, the former chief executive of dairy and drinks business Lion and a former senior executive with Pepsico and Frito-Lay.

Mindshare chief strategy office Joe Lunn said Amazon Australia's share of the food and grocery market was small but growing fast.

"Back in March nobody was buying food and groceries from Amazon whereas ... now 4 per cent of Amazon buyers are buying food and grocery," Mr Lunn told the Financial Review, citing a Mindshare survey conducted last month. "The reality is FMCG [fast moving consumer goods] is still such a small portion of their sales ... but it's opening the door," he said.

Amazon.com.au now has more than 2500 food and grocery products on its site, ranging from packaged foods such as Carman's muesli, Kellogg's corn flakes, Milo milk powder and Mount Franklin mineral water to Finish dishwasher tablets, Omo clothes powder, Huggies nappies and wipes, Colgate toothpaste and Cuddly fabric softener.

Colgate Total toothpaste, for example, costs $3.50 on Amazon.com.au but $7 at Woolworths and Coles, Huggies nappy wipes cost between $2.99 and $3.99 on Amazon compared with $6 at Woolworths and Coles, Omo powder costs $22 compared with $30 at Woolworths and Coles and a 94-pack of Finish dishwasher tablets costs $16.99 versus $35 at Woolworths and Coles.

Some food and beverage prices are also cheaper on Amazon.com including Kellogg's rice bubbles ($3.75 v $6) and Mount Franklin bottled water (20 by 500ml, $5.50 v $6.50 at Woolworths and $9.20 at Coles). After factoring in free delivery through Prime, which is available for most of Amazon's food and grocery items, the price gap is even higher.

However, prices on many other products on Amazon Pantry, such as Nestle's Nescafe Blend 43 ($9.39), Nutella ($3.70), Masterfood chilli powder ($2.90), Arnott's Tim Tams ($2.50) and Dolmio tomato sauce ($2.00) are identical to Woolworths' and Coles'.

Market sources said Amazon was possibly sourcing some international brands through the grey market or parallel imports - a channel Coles and Woolworths have also used to source cheaper stock - pointing to subtle differences in pack sizes and packaging.

If this is the case, it also poses a risk to suppliers if Australian consumers baulk at different flavour profiles and blame the supplier, as they did when discounter Aldi imported Nescafe from Indonesia and Brazil in 2006.

In some instances Amazon's prices are cheaper than the major chains' on leading Australian-made products - such as Carman's fruit and nut muesli (on special at $3.90 on Amazon.com.au, but $5.70 at Woolworths and $5.70 at Coles) - which would not be available through grey channels.

Coles is also understood to be concerned about Amazon's pricing but declined to comment on Thursday.

Former Wesfarmers chief executive Richard Goyder warned two years ago that Amazon, which trades 24 hours a day, seven days a week and can take advantage of its global pricing power, would "eat all our breakfasts, lunches and dinners" unless local retailers lifted their game.

Amazon Australia, which appears to be more concerned about growing sales and customers and passing savings onto shoppers than making a profit, declined to comment on its supply arrangements or whether it was selling food and grocery products at a loss.

"We obsess over the things we believe customers will always care about - low prices, vast selection and fast delivery - and work hard to provide all three, all the time," a spokeswoman said.

HEADLINE: AFR Rich List editors
TEXT: Michael Bailey has been appointed Co-Rich List Editor working with Julie-anne Sprague to compile and produce Australia's leading updates of the nation's wealthy. Bailey was deputy editor of BRW, then editor of BRW.com.au, between 2011 and 2015 and has assisted on the Rich Lists. Since joining the The Australian Financial Review full-time in 2016, he has covered Entrepreneurship and Technology. Bailey will anchor the forthcoming lists while Sprague is on maternity leave.

HEADLINE: Training review short on time
TEXT:
Steven Joyce, the head of the Morrison government's new review into Vocational Education and Training, has just four months to get up to speed and find solutions for the trouble-plagued sector.

Industry and education providers have criticised the short time frame but Mr Joyce has form after reforming the New Zealand VET sector with an emphasis on making it more accountable to students.

"People give up a lot of time and money to be trained, the sector has to be accountable to them," he said.

Mr Joyce described his system overhaul in NZ, which also aimed to introduce more skilled workers into that country's economy, as a "rolling maul" and said New Zealand did not have the "complications and excitements of a federal system".

The former New Zealand minister for education, skills and employment admitted his understanding of the sector in Australia "is not long or detailed" but said "we have to change the way people think about vocational education. It shouldn't be a second chance education. It has to be foundational learning."

The government's aim for Mr Joyce's review is to make sure "Australians have the right skills to succeed in a changing labour market". He has until March to hand in his report with recommendations to fix the ailing sector.

Enrolments in most state-run TAFEs have been falling and private sector providers say they are still struggling to overcome the reputational damage of the VET-Fee Help debacle of 2016. Industry and private providers said the government had given Mr Joyce an "incredibly short" time frame to get his report done.

Australian Industry Group workforce development head Megan Lilly said the review was welcome but needed to focus on university education and the VET sector. The head of TAFE Directors Australia, Craig Robertson, said he was worried the time frame would limit serious consideration of the issues. He said it was only three months since the government had received a review of the vocational education and training act.

HEADLINE: Senate president warns against bill
TEXT:
The Coalition's hopes of passing controversial encryption legislation before Christmas have been dealt a blow after Senate president Scott Ryan warned proposed new powers could conflict with parliamentary privilege.

In a submission to a parliamentary inquiry considering the legislation, Senator Ryan said aspects of the proposal "sits in tension" with work being undertaken to properly secure privilege rules against the exercise of executive investigative powers.

The Morrison government wants Parliament's intelligence committee to complete its inquiry into the bill so the new laws can be passed by next Thursday, the final sitting day for 2018.

In an unusual intervention, Senator Ryan warned expanded powers for covert computer access warrants could deny MPs the chance to make a claim of legal privilege because they could be unaware their information is being accessed. "In that case, Parliament has to rely on the agency seeking the warrant, and the authority approving it, to have proper regard to privilege," the senior Liberal said.

He called for procedural and legislative action to address the issue, and suggested the committee could agree to introduce amendments after the bill passes Parliament if required. Senator Ryan wrote to Attorney-General Christian Porter and Home Affairs Minister Peter Dutton about his concerns this week.

TOM MCILROY

HEADLINE: Nation's rosy budgets at risk from elections
TEXT:
A spending spree in federal and state elections and dependence on volatile housing stamp duties are risks to the public sector's improving fiscal outlook, an independent budget watchdog has warned.

With aggregate state net debt projected to double over the next four years to fund infrastructure and higher public sector wages, the Commonwealth's Parliamentary Budget Office pointed to revenue and spending dangers to state budgets, especially in property-dependent Victoria and NSW.

Overall the independent PBO said the national fiscal outlook - across all levels of government - had improved $24.9 billion since last year's four-year forecast and the nation's public debt would remain low by international standards.

The national net operating balance, which includes federal and state recurrent spending and excludes capital investment, is tipped to improve from a surplus of 0.1 per cent of GDP to a surplus of 2.1 per cent by 2021-22.

The lift is largely driven by the federal government's rising revenues from commodity price-linked corporate tax and GST revenue, as economic growth strengthens.

But the rosy outlook is met by a warning the forecasts exclude the spending commitments in last week's Victorian election and the upcoming NSW and federal elections expected in March and May.

"Rising expenditure beyond projected levels is also a risk, noting in particular that this financial year will see a number of elections take place, increasing the possibility of new spending commitments arising," the PBO said.

"Further, these projections do not factor in any decisions that have been taken since 2018-19 budgets."

The PBO forecasts are largely an accounting exercise, adding up official federal and state budget forecasts published in the first half of this year.

Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews will double Victoria's debt to $80 billion within four years, according to ANZ economists, with debt as a share of the state economy forecast to rise from 6 per cent to 12 per cent of gross state product.

Aggregate debt across all states and territories is projected to reach 5.2 per cent of GDP, the PBO said. The Morrison government has recently unveiled billions of dollars of new spending, including $9 billion in extra GST for the states, $4.5 billion for Catholic and Independent schools, $3.6 billion to bring forward tax cuts for small and medium enterprises and $3.9 billion for a drought fund.

Stephen Anthony, Industry Super Australia chief economist and a former federal Treasury official, said the PBO report signalled that governments were too dependent on temporary cyclical increases in the federal corporate and capital gains tax revenues and state property stamp duties.

"We need to make greater allowance for discretionary spending policy, especially after the recent spend-a-thon in the Victorian election campaign," Mr Anthony said.

An analysis of stamp duty by the PBO shows transfer stamp duty accounted for 15 per cent of aggregate state own-source revenue in 2016-17, with NSW and Victoria accounting for a combined 70 per cent of this state revenue source.

ANZ chief economist Richard Yetsenga forecasts Sydney and Melbourne house prices to fall 15 per cent to 20 per cent from their peaks.

Victorian Treasurer Tim Pallas is counting on a short, shallow housing downturn and a swift return to strong house price growth to support his big spending agenda.

Key pointsThe PBO forecasts are largely an accounting exercise.

Some city house prices are forecast to fall 15 to 20 per cent from their peaks.
